title: Accessibility as a design quality bar
metaTitle: Accessible web design basics as a bar
excerpt: Accessible web design basics are contrast, focus, names, and reduced motion, treated as part of done. WCAG is the reference. A launch is not a certificate.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree. The quiet setup is a reminder that a page should stay readable and operable in ordinary light.
caption: Readable in the room you actually have. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Does shipping an accessible interface mean we are WCAG certified?
faqs.answer: No. WCAG conformance means the content meets the success criteria at a stated level. A studio can design and build toward that standard and still should not hand you a certificate it did not earn through a real evaluation. Ask which checks were done, on which pages, and what was left untested.

faqs.question: What should be true before we call a page done?
faqs.answer: Text should be readable against its background, keyboard focus should be visible, and controls should have names that make sense out of context. Motion should have a reduced version when the person asks for less movement. Those four are a practical bar for a marketing page or a product flow. They do not replace a fuller audit when the product's risk calls for one.

faqs.question: Where do we look this up without hiring a specialist first?
faqs.answer: Start with the W3C's WCAG overview. It explains that WCAG 2.2 is organized into principles and testable success criteria, and that it applies to websites, including mobile. Use it as the reference while you design. Bring in a specialist when you need a conformance claim, a legal review, or help with a flow you cannot assess yourselves.

markdown:
Accessible web design basics are four checks treated as part of done: contrast, keyboard focus, names on controls, and a reduced-motion path. They are not a trailer added the week of launch, and they are not a certificate. The reference is the W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. Meeting a quality bar means you did the checks. Claiming conformance means the relevant success criteria are met, which is a more specific statement and should be made only when it is true.

A founder can hold this bar without becoming a full-time specialist. The bar keeps a page from shipping with gray text, a hidden focus ring, a button named "button," or a carousel that will not sit still. Those failures are design failures. They are visible in the work, and they are cheaper to avoid while the screen is still being drawn.

## The standard, without the costume of a badge

The W3C publishes WCAG as a shared technical standard. Version 2.2 organizes 13 guidelines under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Under the guidelines are testable success criteria at levels A, AA, and AAA. Conformance means meeting those criteria, not resembling a checklist in spirit. The W3C encourages teams to use the latest version. WCAG also applies to web content on mobile, not only to a desktop layout with a magnifying glass nearby.

[The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is explicit that the document is a standard for people who will use the criteria. It is not a gentle introduction, and it is not a logo you paste into a footer. Hanabi uses it as the reference for the quality bar below. The studio does not describe a page as certified because it felt careful. If a project needs a conformance claim, that claim has to name the version, the level, and the pages that were actually evaluated. Anything vaguer is marketing.

You can still design well short of a formal audit. The four checks in this piece sit inside those principles. Contrast and text alternatives support perceivable content. Focus and reduced motion support operable content. Names that say what a control does support understandable content. Robust, in practice, means the name is in the markup a browser and a screen reader can use, not only in a picture of a button.

## Contrast

Text has to be readable against the surface behind it. That includes the quiet gray used for secondary labels, the white text on a photograph, and the placeholder that is doing the job of a label because the label was never drawn. If you squint in ordinary daylight and the words drop out, the contrast is not good enough for the bar, whatever the brand palette prefers.

Photographs are the usual trap. A headline sitting on a busy image will pass on the frame where the sky happened to be empty and fail on the next crop. Put the words on a surface you control, or darken the area behind the words on purpose. Do not rely on a particular photo to be the contrast system.

Do not use color as the only signal. An error that is only a red border, with no text, fails people who cannot see the red and people who are in a hurry. The sentence is the signal. The color can support it. This is the same rule as a form that clears itself and hopes the border was enough. Write the words.

## Focus

Someone who uses a keyboard, or a switch, or simply tabs through a form, needs to see where they are. The focus indicator has to be visible against the control and against the page. Removing the outline because it clashes with a mock is a defect. Design a focus style that belongs to the product, and check it by tabbing, not by looking at a static frame.

Order follows the order of the work. Tabbing should meet the fields in the sequence a person fills them, and it should reach the primary action. A decorative element that steals focus, or a menu that traps focus until an invisible control is found, is not done. Test the menu the way you test the happy path. Open it, move through it, close it, and confirm you can keep going.

Skip links and headings help on longer pages. A marketing page with one topic may not need a complicated skip pattern. It still needs headings in an order that matches the outline, so a person who navigates by heading is not walking through a pile of divs. Structure is an accessibility decision even when nobody on the team uses a screen reader every day.

## Names

Every control needs a name that makes sense if the visual layout disappears. "Submit" on one button and "Submit" on another, with the difference only in a nearby heading, is a weak name. "Send invoice" and "Save draft" survive being read as a list. Icons without a text name do not. If the picture is the only label, the name is missing, even if the picture is beautiful.

Images that carry information need a text alternative that says what the information is. Decorative images can be marked so they are skipped. Alt text that repeats the headline, or that stuffs a keyword, fails both the person and the page. Write it when you place the image, while you can still see the crop.

Form fields need labels that stay visible. A placeholder is a hint, and it vanishes. The label is the name. Group related fields when the group has a meaning, such as a billing address, so the name of each field is not just "line 1" spoken with no context. This is ordinary interface work. It is also the work that makes the form understandable, which is one of the four principles, applied to a screen you were going to ship anyway.

## Reduced motion

Some people ask their system to reduce motion because movement makes them sick, distracted, or unable to read. A page that only exists as a sequence of entrances has ignored that request. Ship two versions of a move: the one you intended, and a still or instant version when reduced motion is requested. Information should not depend on the longer version. If a diagram only makes sense while it animates, the diagram is incomplete.

Autoplaying carousels and parallax that shove content around fail the same bar. If something must move to show a relationship, keep it short, let it be dismissed or avoided, and honor the reduced-motion request. Hanabi treats this as part of the craft of a marketing site, not as an advanced setting. The still page has to be coherent. Motion may add a relationship. It may not be the only way to understand the offer.

## Put the bar in the definition of done

Add the four checks to the review you already hold before launch. Tab the page. Read the names. Look at the text on the real background. Turn on reduced motion and reload. Do this on the template and on one real page with real content, because a component can pass in isolation and fail in a photograph. Write down what you did not check. An honest gap is more useful than a footer badge.

When the product grows into flows that handle money, accounts, or other high-stakes tasks, plan a fuller pass against the success criteria, with someone who will tell you what failed. The everyday bar does not expire at that point. It remains the minimum for every new screen, so the audit is not the first time anyone looked.

The motion half of this bar has its own detail: how to design the reduced path so it still feels considered. That piece is [reduced motion is part of the craft](/blog/reduced-motion).

If you want the bar held while the interface is designed and built, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio treats contrast, focus, names, and reduced motion as part of done, and points at WCAG as the reference rather than as a sticker.
